title: Customer Commitment Conveyor and Signal Calibration Playbook
creator: Priya Shah
description:
Problem: As Redwood scales, we receive heterogeneous signals from strategic customers (feature requests, SLA asks, quantitative telemetry) that are hard to compare and route into engineering cycles reliably. Without a standardized conveyor to normalize signals and tie them to commitment SLOs, PMs over-rotate on individual escalations or miss cross-customer value.

Goal: Build a lightweight, repeatable playbook + intake pipeline (the 'Commitment Conveyor') that: 1) normalizes customer signals into calibrated scores, 2) maps scores to commitment SLAs (acknowledge/response/runway), 3) surfaces mechanistic actions (rapid experiments, customer pilots, roadmap tickets), and 4) provides observable commitments (owner, date, and success metric) so Sales/CS have predictable expectations.

Scope: This ticket covers the playbook, scoring rubric, routing rules, SLO definitions for 'Committed', 'Evaluating', 'Queued', and the minimal Console dashboard mock for internal stakeholders. Implementation of full automation (forms + routing) will be a follow-up (sub-issue).
acceptance_criteria: Calibrated scoring rubric documented and accepted by PM, Eng lead, and CS lead
Commitment SLOs defined (acknowledge within 3 business days, roadmap admission window defined) and published internally
Routing matrix mapping score bands to actions (Pilot / Experiment / Roadmap / Decline) with responsible owners
Console mock that lists active commitments with owner, deadline, success metric and status (mock link in artifacts) approved by stakeholders
Rollout communication plan and CS/Sales playbook ready for pilot accounts

risks_and_tradeoffs: Overfitting the rubric to revenue may de-prioritize high-risk technical or compliance work that affects multiple customers
Publishing commitment dates increases expectation pressure; need guardrails to avoid SLA violations and legal commitments
Heavy automation early could create noisy routing; starting with a human-in-the-loop process reduces false positives
Tight SLO windows (e.g., guaranteed delivery dates) may be infeasible given model/infra uncertainty; prefer stage-based commitments
